questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 3-year-old boy presents with episodic, painless rectal bleeding. A Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focal area of uptake in the right iliac fossa, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve. Surgery reveals a blind-ending ileal diverticulum lined with gastric mucosa. Which embryological structure failed to obliterate?
questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the GI tract, resulting from persistence of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct. It follows the rule of 2s: occurs in 2% of population, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, presents before age 2, and may contain 2 types of ectopic mucosa (gastric or pancreatic). Gastric mucosa secretes acid, causing peptic ulceration and painless rectal bleeding — the classic presentation. Technetium-99m pertechnetate scans for gastric mucosa ('Meckel's scan'). Option A (Allantois) → urachal remnants (median umbilical ligament, urachal cyst/sinus/fistula). Option B (Urachus) → same as allantois, causing umbilical discharge of urine. Option D (Secondary yolk sac) → not associated with any clinically significant remnant structure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A neonate is found to have choanal atresia, coloboma of the retina, heart defect (VSD), genital hypoplasia, and ear anomalies. The genetic basis involves deletion of chromosome 22q11. Which pharyngeal pouch derivative is most likely absent in this condition?
questions.explanation: This is DiGeorge syndrome (CHARGE association overlaps, but the 22q11.2 deletion is classic DiGeorge). The 3rd pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands and thymus. In DiGeorge syndrome, failure of 3rd (and sometimes 4th) pouch development leads to thymic aplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency) and hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia, tetany). Option A: 1st pouch → Eustachian tube and middle ear cavity — present in DiGeorge. Option B: 2nd pouch → palatine tonsil fossa — also present. Option D: 4th pouch → superior parathyroid — may be partially affected but the hallmark is 3rd pouch loss. Exam pearl: 22q11 deletion is the most common microdeletion syndrome; CATCH-22 mnemonic — Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A fetus is found on echocardiography to have transposition of the great arteries (TGA). Neural crest cells failed to migrate adequately to the cardiac outflow tract. Which septum, formed by spiraling of the outflow tract, is defective in TGA?
questions.explanation: The aorticopulmonary (AP) septum forms by the spiraling of neural crest cell-derived mesenchyme in the truncus arteriosus and conus cordis, dividing the outflow tract into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Normal spiraling (270°) results in the aorta arising from the left ventricle and pulmonary trunk from the right. In TGA, the AP septum fails to spiral (grows straight), resulting in the aorta arising from the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk from the left — parallel circulation incompatible with extrauterine life without a mixing defect (ASD/VSD/PDA). Option A: Septum primum → separates left and right atria; defect → ASD. Option C: Membranous IV septum → formed by merging of AP septum with endocardial cushions; isolated defect → perimembranous VSD. Option D: Endocardial cushions → separate AV valves; defect → AV canal/AVSD (common in Down syndrome). Exam trap: Do not confuse TGA (AP septum defect) with Tetralogy of Fallot (also AP septum, but shifts anterosuperiorly causing unequal division).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A baby girl is born with bilateral renal agenesis confirmed on post-natal imaging. Pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened face (Potter facies), and limb deformities are noted. The primary embryological failure responsible for the pulmonary hypoplasia is:

options.A: Failure of ureteric bud to develop
options.B: Oligohydramnios causing reduced fetal breathing movements
options.C: Direct compression of lung buds by the absent kidneys

questions.explanation: Potter sequence results from bilateral renal agenesis → no fetal urine production → oligohydramnios → reduced fetal breathing movements → pulmonary hypoplasia. Normally, fetal swallowing and breathing of amniotic fluid (which contains fetal urine) is critical for lung development. Oligohydramnios also causes external compression by uterine walls → Potter facies (flat nose, low-set ears, epicanthal folds) and limb deformities (clubfoot). Option A describes the mechanism of renal agenesis itself (ureteric bud fails to meet metanephric mesenchyme), not pulmonary hypoplasia. Option C is incorrect — absent kidneys do not directly compress lung buds. Option D also describes the renal agenesis mechanism. The cascade is: Renal agenesis → oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia + Potter facies + limb deformity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.image_title: MRI Brain of a Newborn with Lissencephaly
key_findings: Smooth brain surface without gyri or sulci (agyria)
Thickened cortex (>10mm)
Figure-of-8 appearance on axial cuts
Enlarged sylvian fissures
Normal posterior fossa
questions.question_text: A newborn's MRI brain is shown above. The brain shows a smooth surface without gyri or sulci. This appearance is due to failure of which process during cortical development?

options.B: Neuronal proliferation in the ventricular zone
options.C: Neuronal migration from ventricular zone to cortical plate

questions.explanation: Lissencephaly ('smooth brain') results from failure of neuronal migration. Neurons originate in the ventricular/subventricular zone and migrate outward along radial glial fibers to form the six-layered neocortex. Failure of migration results in a thick, disorganized cortex with absent gyri (agyria) or sparse broad gyri (pachygyria). Genes involved: LIS1, DCX (doublecortin — X-linked, more common in males). Option A: Neural tube closure failure → anencephaly or spina bifida, not lissencephaly. Option B: Neuronal proliferation failure → microcephaly (fewer neurons) or megalencephaly (too many). Option D: Myelination failure → leukodystrophies (white matter disease), not cortical gyral pattern. Exam pearl: 'Inside-out' migration — last neurons to migrate end up in the outermost (most superficial) cortical layer. In lissencephaly, this process is arrested, causing cortical disorganization.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old construction worker falls from scaffolding and sustains a hyperabduction injury to his right arm. Examination reveals: inability to abduct the arm beyond 15° (supraspinatus), loss of external rotation, absent biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, and preserved hand intrinsics. The pattern of neurological deficit is most consistent with injury to which roots?
questions.explanation: This is classic Erb's palsy (C5, C6 injury). The mechanism is violent separation of the head from the shoulder (birth — traction on neck; adults — motorcycle accidents, falls). Structures denervated: Supraspinatus (C5, C6) → cannot initiate abduction; Infraspinatus (C5, C6) → lost external rotation; Biceps brachii (C5, C6) → absent biceps reflex; Brachioradialis (C6) → absent brachioradialis reflex. The 'waiter's tip' posture results: arm medially rotated, adducted, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist flexed. Hand intrinsics are preserved because they are C8, T1. Option A (C8, T1 / Klumpke's) → causes claw hand (intrinsic minus), wrist drop is not present; Horner's syndrome if T1 ramus communicans involved. Option C (C7) → triceps weakness, wrist drop; reflexes — triceps absent. Option D (Posterior cord) → axillary + radial nerve territory; deltoid palsy + wrist drop but no biceps weakness.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man sustains a stab wound at the medial epicondyle of the humerus. He develops clawing of the ring and little fingers, inability to abduct/adduct fingers, loss of sensation over the medial 1½ fingers and hypothenar eminence, and weakness of wrist flexion with ulnar deviation. Which nerve is injured and at what level?

options.C: Ulnar nerve at the wrist (Guyon's canal)
options.D: Radial nerve at the spiral groove

questions.explanation: Ulnar nerve injury at the elbow (cubital tunnel/medial epicondyle) causes: Clawing of 4th and 5th digits (more pronounced than at wrist — 'ulnar paradox'), weakness of flexor carpi ulnaris (wrist flexion with radial deviation) and medial two FDP, wasted hypothenar and interossei, loss of finger abduction/adduction, and sensory loss over medial 1½ fingers including dorsal surface (dorsal cutaneous branch arises above wrist, so dorsal sensory is also lost with elbow injury). 'Ulnar paradox': Injury at the wrist produces MORE clawing because FDP (which flexes the IP joints) is intact at wrist level, exaggerating the claw. Injury at the elbow — FDP to 4th/5th fingers is also weak, reducing IP flexion and thus reducing paradoxically the severity of clawing. Option A: Median at wrist → 'Pope's blessing' (1st/2nd digits cannot flex), thenar wasting, no ring/little finger clawing. Option C: Ulnar at Guyon's canal → hypothenar + intrinsic weakness, but dorsal sensation preserved and FCU intact. Option D: Radial at spiral groove → wrist drop, loss of finger/thumb extension, spared brachioradialis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old woman complains of shoulder pain and inability to initiate abduction of the arm. She can abduct if the arm is passively lifted beyond 15°. MRI reveals a full-thickness tear of the superior rotator cuff. Which muscle is most likely torn, and what is its nerve supply?

options.C: Subscapularis — upper and lower subscapular nerves

questions.explanation: Supraspinatus initiates the first 15° of shoulder abduction (0–15°) and acts synergistically with deltoid thereafter. A full-thickness supraspinatus tear results in inability to initiate abduction; once the arm is passively brought past 15°, deltoid (axillary nerve, C5, C6) can continue. The supraspinatus lies in the supraspinous fossa and is innervated by the suprascapular nerve (C5, C6), which passes through the suprascapular notch (inferior to superior transverse scapular ligament — 'Army goes under the bridge': nerve under ligament; suprascapular artery over it). Option A: Infraspinatus also receives suprascapular nerve but is the chief external rotator, not abductor. Option C: Subscapularis is the chief internal rotator (tests — lift-off test, belly-press test). Option D: Teres minor — external rotation (tested in quadrangular space syndrome). Exam pearl: SITS mnemonic for rotator cuff — Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A pianist develops carpal tunnel syndrome. Surgical decompression is planned. Which structure forms the floor and roof of the carpal tunnel respectively?
questions.explanation: The carpal tunnel is an osseofibrous canal at the wrist. Floor and sides: concave anterior surface of carpal bones (forming the carpal groove). Roof: flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament). Contents: Median nerve (most superficial and lateral, compressed first in CTS), FPL tendon (1), FDS tendons (4), FDP tendons (4) — total 9 tendons + 1 nerve = 10 structures. The flexor carpi radialis passes in its own fibrous tunnel within the retinaculum. Palmaris longus, ulnar nerve, and ulnar vessels pass superficial to the retinaculum (NOT within the carpal tunnel). Option B is incorrect — flexor retinaculum is the roof, not floor. Options C and D have the structures wrongly assigned. Exam pearl: Surgical decompression involves cutting the flexor retinaculum (the roof) — opening the carpal tunnel relieves median nerve compression. Recurrent branch of median nerve exits at the distal edge of retinaculum and enters thenar eminence — 'the million dollar nerve' (must be preserved during surgery).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 70-year-old woman falls on her outstretched hand and subsequently develops severe right groin pain. X-ray reveals a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. She develops avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head 6 months later. The artery most responsible for supplying the femoral head in adults, damage to which causes AVN, is:
questions.explanation: The blood supply to the femoral head is critical and age-dependent. In adults, the dominant supply comes from the medial circumflex femoral artery (MCFA), a branch of the profunda femoris. Its retinacular (ascending cervical) branches ascend along the femoral neck beneath the retinaculum of Weitbrecht and enter the femoral head at the articular margin. An intracapsular femoral neck fracture disrupts these retinacular vessels → AVN of femoral head (rate: ~30% for Garden III/IV fractures). Option A: Artery of ligamentum teres (from obturator artery) is dominant only in children (up to age 7); in adults it is a minor supply. Option C: Lateral circumflex femoral artery supplies the greater trochanter and anastomoses but contributes minimally to the femoral head in adults. Option D: Inferior gluteal artery does not directly supply the femoral head. Exam pearl: Garden classification of femoral neck fractures — Grade I (incomplete, valgus impacted), II (complete, undisplaced), III (complete, partial displacement), IV (complete displacement). Grades III and IV have highest risk of AVN.

questions.subject: Anatomy
key_findings: Disruption of the anterior cruciate ligament fibers on sagittal T2
Bone bruise at lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau
Joint effusion (bright T2 signal)
Posterior cruciate ligament intact
Medial meniscus appears intact
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old football player hears a 'pop' in his right knee, develops immediate swelling, and is unable to continue playing. The MRI is shown above. On examination, anterior drawer and Lachman tests are positive. The injured ligament primarily prevents which movement?

options.A: Posterior translation of tibia on femur
options.B: Anterior translation of tibia on femur

questions.explanation: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) runs from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle (LMAF mnemonic: Lateral Medial Anterior Femur). Its primary function is to prevent anterior translation of the tibia on the femur (or posterior translation of femur on tibia). The ACL also prevents hyperextension and limits internal rotation. Clinical tests: Anterior drawer (90° flexion), Lachman test (20–30° flexion — more sensitive than anterior drawer), Pivot shift test. Bone bruise at lateral femoral condyle + posterolateral tibial plateau is pathognomonic for ACL tear (kissing contusions — the tibia pivots forward striking the femoral condyle). Option A: PCL prevents posterior tibial translation; tested by posterior drawer/sag sign. Option C: Valgus stress is resisted by the medial collateral ligament (MCL). Option D: External tibial rotation is limited by the LCL and posterolateral corner structures. Exam pearl: Unhappy triad (O'Donoghue) — ACL + MCL + medial meniscus tear from valgus force. Modern MRI often shows lateral meniscus is more commonly torn in ACL injuries.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman undergoes total hip replacement (posterior approach). Three weeks postoperatively, she develops foot drop and difficulty dorsiflexing the ankle. She also has loss of sensation over the dorsum of foot and lateral leg. Which nerve was most likely injured during surgery?
questions.explanation: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve is the most commonly injured nerve during posterior total hip replacement. It winds around the fibular neck and is vulnerable to traction/compression. Injury causes: Foot drop (weak dorsiflexion and eversion of foot — deep and superficial peroneal branches), sensory loss over dorsum of foot and lateral leg (superficial peroneal), high-stepping gait. Differentiating peroneal from sciatic nerve injury at hip: Sciatic nerve injury → both peroneal AND tibial distributions (plantarflexion, toe flexion also lost + sole sensory). Option A: Femoral nerve → loss of knee extension (quadriceps), hip flexion, absent patellar reflex, anteromedial thigh/leg sensory loss. Option C: Tibial nerve → loss of plantarflexion, toe flexion, absent ankle jerk, plantar sensory loss; causes calcaneovalgus (opposite of foot drop). Option D: Superior gluteal nerve → gluteus medius/minimus weakness → Trendelenburg gait; no foot drop. Exam pearl: The peroneal division of the sciatic nerve is MORE prone to injury than the tibial division because it is more tightly tethered at the fibular neck and has less connective tissue padding.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A patient develops a pseudo-aneurysm of the femoral artery following cardiac catheterization. The femoral artery is cannulated in the femoral triangle. Which statement about the contents of the femoral triangle, from lateral to medial, is correct?

options.A: Nerve — Artery — Vein — Empty space — Lymphatics (NAVEL)
options.B: Artery — Vein — Nerve — Empty space — Lymphatics

questions.explanation: The femoral triangle contents from lateral to medial are: Nerve (femoral nerve, most lateral), Artery (femoral artery), Vein (femoral vein), Empty space, Lymphatics (deep inguinal lymph nodes and lymphatics). Mnemonic: NAVEL — Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics. The femoral sheath (derived from transversalis fascia anteriorly and iliac fascia posteriorly) encloses only the femoral artery, vein, and lymphatics in three compartments — NOT the femoral nerve (which lies lateral to the sheath). The medial compartment (femoral canal) contains the lymph node of Cloquet (Rosenmüller) and is the site of femoral hernia. Boundaries of femoral triangle: base = inguinal ligament, medial = adductor longus, lateral = sartorius, roof = fascia lata, floor = iliopsoas and pectineus. Option B, C, D are incorrect arrangements. Exam pearl: Femoral canal is the weak point where femoral hernia occurs — passes through the femoral ring, medial to femoral vein. Femoral hernias are more common in women (wider pelvis) but inguinal hernias are still more common overall in both sexes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male smoker presents with left-sided Pancoast tumor at the apex of the lung. He develops ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the left side. In addition to Horner's syndrome, he has wasting of the small muscles of the left hand. Which structures are being compressed by the tumor?

options.A: Cervical sympathetic chain and C8, T1 nerve roots
options.B: Brachial plexus upper trunk (C5, C6) and phrenic nerve
options.C: Recurrent laryngeal nerve and vagus nerve

questions.explanation: Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumor is an apical lung tumor that invades adjacent structures. The classic triad involves: Cervical sympathetic chain (T1 preganglionic fibers to superior cervical ganglion) → Horner's syndrome: ptosis (Müller's muscle), miosis (dilator pupillae), anhidrosis (facial sweat glands), and enophthalmos. C8, T1 nerve roots (lower trunk of brachial plexus) → Klumpke-type wasting of small hand muscles (interossei, hypothenar, thenar — ulnar and median intrinsics). Sometimes also: Subclavian artery — vascular compromise; Recurrent laryngeal nerve — hoarseness. Option B: Upper trunk (C5, C6) involvement → shoulder/proximal arm weakness, not hand wasting. Option C: Recurrent laryngeal nerve and vagus → hoarseness and autonomic features, not hand wasting. Option D: Phrenic nerve compression → ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis (elevated hemidiaphragm on CXR). Exam pearl: Pancoast tumor = Horner's + hand muscle wasting = pathognomonic of superior sulcus involvement. CXR shows apical opacity with rib destruction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male presents with progressive dysphagia to solids. Barium swallow shows compression of the esophagus by a posterior mediastinal mass. CT reveals an enlarged lymph node compressing the esophagus at the level of T4–T5. This corresponds to which anatomical landmark?

options.A: Level of the sternal angle (angle of Louis)
options.D: Level of the carina of the trachea

questions.explanation: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is the junction between the manubrium and body of sternum. It is the most clinically important thoracic landmark, located at the level of T4–T5 intervertebral disc. Structures at this level: Bifurcation of trachea (carina), Bifurcation of pulmonary trunk, Start of aortic arch (and its termination), Junction of superior and inferior mediastinum, Entry of azygos vein into SVC, Crossing of thoracic duct from right to left, 2nd rib articulation with sternum (clinical landmark for counting ribs). Dysphagia at this level suggests compression at tracheal bifurcation — lymph nodes at the carina (subcarinal) or paratracheal region. Option B: Xiphisternal joint → T9 level; lower mediastinum. Option C: Cricoid → C6; transition from pharynx to esophagus/larynx to trachea. Option D: The carina IS at the level of the sternal angle (T4–T5), so this answer is partially correct structurally, but Option A is the anatomical surface landmark being asked. The question asks for the anatomical landmark matching the CT level of T4–T5. Exam pearl: Sternal angle = T4–T5 = Superior/inferior mediastinum boundary = Carina level = Aortic arch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man undergoes coronary angiography. The dominant coronary artery (right coronary in 85% of people) supplies the AV node. The AV node artery most commonly arises from which branch?

options.B: Marginal branch of right coronary artery

questions.explanation: The AV nodal artery is a branch of the posterior descending artery (PDA), which itself arises from the right coronary artery in right-dominant circulation (85%). Hence, RCA occlusion can cause: AV block (AV nodal ischemia), Inferior STEMI (PDA territory — posterior IV septum, inferior wall of LV). SA nodal artery also arises predominantly from the RCA (60%) — RCA occlusion may also cause sinus node dysfunction. Option A: LAD supplies AV bundle (Bundle of His), right bundle branch, and anterior left bundle branch — LAD occlusion causes bundle branch blocks. Option B: Marginal branch of RCA → right ventricular free wall. Option D: Left circumflex → lateral wall of LV, may give SA node artery in 40% (left-dominant or co-dominant). Exam pearl: In inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF), always check for AV block — indicates RCA occlusion proximal to AV nodal branch. Temporary pacing may be needed.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man is referred for investigation of heartburn and regurgitation. Endoscopy reveals a sliding hiatus hernia. The esophagus traverses the diaphragm through the esophageal hiatus, accompanied by which structures?

options.A: Vagal trunks and esophageal branches of left gastric artery
options.D: Inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve

questions.explanation: Three major diaphragmatic openings and their contents (mnemonic — 'I Ate Ten'): Inferior vena cava (T8) → IVC and right phrenic nerve. Esophageal hiatus (T10) → Esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks (left vagus becomes anterior at hiatus), and esophageal branches of left gastric vessels. Aortic hiatus (T12) → Aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein. T8 = IVC (caval = 8 letters), T10 = Esophagus (esophagus = 10 letters), T12 = Aorta (aorta = 5... just remember 12 = aorta). In sliding hiatus hernia, the gastroesophageal junction and part of stomach slides through the esophageal hiatus into the posterior mediastinum. Option B: Thoracic duct passes through aortic hiatus at T12. Option C: Aorta and thoracic duct are at T12. Option D: IVC and right phrenic nerve pass through the caval opening at T8. Exam pearl: Rolling (para-esophageal) hernia — gastric fundus herniates alongside esophagus, GEJ remains below diaphragm; risk of volvulus. Sliding hernia — GEJ moves above diaphragm; more common, causes GERD.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old male presents with a reducible groin swelling that appears above and medial to the pubic tubercle. On examination, the swelling does not transilluminate. When reduced and the deep ring is occluded by finger pressure, the hernia does not reappear on Valsalva. Which type of hernia does this describe, and what is its relationship to the inferior epigastric vessels?

options.A: Direct inguinal hernia — medial to inferior epigastric vessels, through Hesselbach's triangle
options.B: Indirect inguinal hernia — lateral to inferior epigastric vessels, through deep inguinal ring
options.C: Femoral hernia — below and lateral to pubic tubercle
options.D: Spigelian hernia — at the lateral edge of rectus abdominis

questions.explanation: The swelling above and medial to the pubic tubercle is an inguinal hernia (femoral hernia would be below and lateral to pubic tubercle). When the deep ring is compressed and the hernia does not reappear → direct inguinal hernia (because it does not pass through the deep ring; it protrudes directly through Hesselbach's/inguinal triangle). Direct hernia: passes medial to inferior epigastric vessels through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach's triangle — bounded by inguinal ligament, inferior epigastric vessels, and lateral edge of rectus abdominis). Indirect hernia: passes lateral to inferior epigastric vessels through the deep inguinal ring, traverses the entire inguinal canal, and exits at the superficial ring; may descend into the scrotum. Compressing deep ring controls indirect but NOT direct. Direct hernias are acquired (weakness of transversalis fascia), rarely strangulate. Indirect hernias are congenital (patent processus vaginalis) or acquired, more likely to strangulate. Option B describes indirect. Option C describes femoral hernia (below inguinal ligament, through femoral canal). Option D describes Spigelian hernia — interparietal hernia through semilunar line. Exam pearl: All hernias above and medial to pubic tubercle = inguinal. Below and lateral = femoral.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old alcoholic with cirrhosis develops hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals large esophageal varices. These varices form due to portosystemic anastomosis between which vessels?

options.A: Left gastric vein (portal) and azygos/hemiazygos tributaries (systemic) at the lower esophagus
options.B: Superior mesenteric vein and inferior vena cava directly
options.C: Para-umbilical veins (portal) and superficial epigastric veins (systemic)
options.D: Inferior mesenteric vein and left renal vein

questions.explanation: Portosystemic anastomoses form when portal hypertension shunts blood through primitive connections: (1) Esophageal varices: Left gastric vein (portal tributaries) ↔ esophageal tributaries of azygos/hemiazygos (systemic) — most clinically dangerous; can cause life-threatening hematemesis. (2) Hemorrhoidal varices: Superior rectal vein (IMV → portal) ↔ middle and inferior rectal veins (internal iliac → systemic). (3) Caput medusae: Para-umbilical veins (portal) ↔ superficial and inferior epigastric veins (systemic) — visible at umbilicus. (4) Retroperitoneal (veins of Retzius): Portal tributaries ↔ caval tributaries behind the colon. Option B: SMV does not anastomose with IVC directly under physiological circumstances. Option C describes caput medusae — para-umbilical, not esophageal varices. Option D: IMV to left renal vein is a naturally occurring shunt (spleno-renal) used surgically, not a natural anastomosis causing varices. Exam pearl: In cirrhosis, remember 3 clinical manifestations of portosystemic shunting — esophageal varices (hematemesis), caput medusae (umbilical), hemorrhoids (rectal); plus hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia bypasses liver).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old male presents with right iliac fossa pain. McBurney's point tenderness is present. Rovsing's sign is positive. The base of the appendix is located at McBurney's point. What is the exact surface marking of McBurney's point?

options.A: Junction of lateral 1/3 and medial 2/3 of a line from ASIS to umbilicus
options.B: Junction of medial 1/3 and lateral 2/3 of a line from ASIS to umbilicus
options.C: Midpoint of the right inguinal ligament
options.D: 2 cm above and medial to the right ASIS

questions.explanation: McBurney's point is located at the junction of the medial 1/3 and lateral 2/3 of a line drawn from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus. This is the surface marking for the base of the appendix (where it arises from the cecum at the confluence of the taeniae coli). This distinction (medial 1/3 from ASIS side, lateral 2/3 from umbilical side) is frequently confused — McBurney's point is closer to the ASIS than the umbilicus (i.e., lies 2/3 of the way from the umbilicus, or 1/3 of the way from the ASIS). Option A reverses the fractions — junction of lateral 1/3 and medial 2/3 would place it closer to the umbilicus, which is incorrect. Option C: Midpoint of inguinal ligament → surface marking for femoral artery pulsation. Option D: Not a standard anatomical landmark. Exam pearl: Rovsing's sign — pressure on LIF causes pain in RIF (due to gas shifting in colon pressing on inflamed peritoneum). Lanz point (variation) — junction of right and middle thirds of the bi-iliac line. Appendix tip position varies: retrocecal (most common, 65%), pelvic (30%), pre-ileal, post-ileal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is planned for a right-sided renal calculus. The surgeon performs the puncture through the posterior aspect at the lower pole. Which structure is at greatest risk of injury during this procedure?

options.A: Pleura (costophrenic recess) when puncturing above the 12th rib
options.B: Peritoneum on the anterior surface of the kidney
options.C: Duodenum (second part) anterior to the right kidney
options.D: Inferior vena cava medial to the right kidney

questions.explanation: During PCNL, puncture is typically made below the 12th rib (lower pole) or between the 11th and 12th ribs (upper/mid pole). The key risk of upper-pole puncture is injury to the pleura and lung (costophrenic angle of pleura extends to level of 12th rib posteriorly, 10th rib midaxillary, 8th rib midclavicular). Supra-12th rib puncture risks pneumothorax, hydrothorax, or hemothorax. Other structures at risk: Posteriorly — subcostal nerve (T12), iliohypogastric (L1), ilioinguinal (L1) nerves, crossing behind the kidney. Anteriorly — on the RIGHT: duodenum (2nd part), hepatic flexure of colon, liver. On the LEFT: spleen, jejunum, splenic flexure. A posterior approach through the avascular plane of Brodel (between anterior 2/3 and posterior 1/3 blood supply) minimizes bleeding. Option B: Peritoneum is at risk only if the approach deviates anteriorly. Option C and D are structures at risk of anterior injuries, not direct posterior puncture risks for lower-pole access. Exam pearl: The right kidney is lower than the left (displaced by liver). Both kidneys are retroperitoneal. The hilum faces anteromedially, located at L1 (right) and L1–L2 (left).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old diabetic man presents with sudden onset of right-sided headache behind the eye, diplopia with inability to look down and in (intorted adduction), and a dilated, non-reactive right pupil. MRI shows a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing CN III. In this condition, why is the pupil involved early?

options.A: Pupillomotor fibers run in the center of CN III and are supplied by the deep perforating arteries
options.B: Pupillomotor fibers run on the outer surface of CN III and are compressed first by the aneurysm
options.C: Pupillomotor fibers are carried by CN VI and are compressed at the cavernous sinus
options.D: Diabetic ischemia preferentially affects pupillomotor fibers

questions.explanation: The pupillomotor (parasympathetic) fibers of CN III originate from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus and travel on the outer (superficial, dorsomedial) surface of the oculomotor nerve. This is critical — external compression (e.g., by a PComm aneurysm, uncal herniation) affects these superficial fibers FIRST, causing pupil dilation (mydriasis) before extraocular muscle weakness. This is 'surgical' third nerve palsy: PAINFUL, pupil-involving. In contrast, 'medical' (diabetic, hypertensive) CN III palsy: PAINLESS, pupil-SPARING. This is because diabetic ischemia affects the central core of the nerve (somatic motor fibers) while sparing superficial pupillomotor fibers (which have better external microvascular supply). Option A is exactly wrong — superficial, not central. Option C: Pupillomotor fibers are within CN III, not CN VI. Option D: Diabetic ischemia SPARES pupil — opposite of what's described. Exam trap: Pupil-sparing CN III palsy = medical (ischemic); Pupil-involving CN III palsy = surgical emergency (aneurysm) — warrants urgent angiography!

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy. She develops hoarseness immediately postoperatively. The nerve most likely injured, and the consequence of its bilateral injury, is:

options.A: External laryngeal nerve — bilateral injury causes voice fatigue but not hoarseness
options.B: Recurrent laryngeal nerve — bilateral injury causes respiratory distress requiring tracheostomy
options.C: Internal laryngeal nerve — bilateral injury causes loss of laryngeal sensation
options.D: Glossopharyngeal nerve — bilateral injury causes dysphagia

questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) is the most commonly injured nerve during thyroid surgery. It runs in the tracheoesophageal groove and enters the larynx posteriorly, supplying all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid (which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve). Unilateral RLN injury → ipsilateral vocal cord paralysis → hoarseness (the cord lies in the paramedian or lateral position, unable to adduct fully for phonation). Bilateral RLN injury → both cords lie in paramedian position due to unopposed cricothyroid action → the cords come together narrowing the glottis → respiratory distress, stridor, and may need emergency tracheostomy. The RLN loops: right RLN hooks around the right subclavian artery; left RLN loops around the aortic arch (ligamentum arteriosum) — hence left RLN has a longer intrathoracic course and is more at risk from mediastinal pathology. Option A: External laryngeal nerve injury → loss of cricothyroid function → voice loses high pitch/power (singer's nerve); does not cause hoarseness per se. Option C: Internal laryngeal nerve → sensory to supraglottis; injury → aspiration risk, not hoarseness. Option D: Glossopharyngeal → pharyngeal sensation; not involved in thyroid surgery. Exam pearl: The RLN is close to the inferior thyroid artery — surgical identification of the RLN is mandatory before ligation of the inferior thyroid artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man undergoes superficial parotidectomy for a pleomorphic adenoma. Postoperatively, he develops Frey's syndrome — flushing and sweating over the cheek during meals. The nerve responsible for this aberrant reinnervation is:
questions.explanation: Frey's syndrome (auriculotemporal nerve syndrome) results from aberrant regeneration of parasympathetic secretomotor fibers of the auriculotemporal nerve into the sweat glands and cutaneous vessels of the skin overlying the parotid. Normally: Auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers (from otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve → parotid gland for secretion) and somatosensory fibers to the skin of the temple and preauricular area. After parotidectomy, the auriculotemporal nerve fibers regenerate aberrantly to innervate sweat glands and cutaneous vasculature. When the patient eats (stimulus for salivation), parasympathetic impulses are sent through the misdirected fibers → gustatory sweating and flushing (Frey's syndrome). Option A: Facial nerve branches provide motor supply; their injury causes facial weakness but not Frey's syndrome. Option C: Great auricular nerve (C2, C3) provides cutaneous sensation; not involved in Frey's syndrome. Option D: Lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the otic ganglion; it is the presynaptic component, not responsible for aberrant regeneration. Exam pearl: The auriculotemporal nerve — V3 branch — hooks around the middle meningeal artery in the infratemporal fossa and carries postganglionic parasympathetics from the otic ganglion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man presents with septic thrombosis of the cavernous sinus following facial cellulitis. He develops proptosis, periorbital edema, chemosis, and a painful ophthalmoplegia. Which cranial nerve, running within the wall of the cavernous sinus (NOT within the lumen), would be the LAST to be affected?
questions.explanation: Contents of the cavernous sinus — mnemonic 'O TOM CAT': In the lateral wall (from superior to inferior): O = Oculomotor (CN III), T = Trochlear (CN IV), O = Ophthalmic (V1), M = Maxillary (V2). In the lumen (within the blood): C = Carotid artery (internal), A = Abducens (CN VI). Because CN VI runs freely within the sinus lumen (surrounded by venous blood), it is the MOST IMMEDIATELY affected by thrombosis (earliest ophthalmoplegia = lateral gaze palsy, inability to abduct the eye). However, the question asks which nerve in the WALL (not lumen) is LAST to be affected. The walls contain CN III, IV, V1, V2 (in order from superior to inferior). CN V2 (maxillary) is in the inferolateral wall and would be last among the wall nerves. But among the answer options given, CN VI is technically in the lumen (not the wall) — the question asks about wall nerves specifically. Among wall nerves in options: CN VI (actually in lumen); the last WALL nerve affected would be V1 as it is most protected inferolaterally. However, in standard exam context: CN VI is most commonly first affected (lumen) and V1/V2 last (wall). The answer is D because CN VI's involvement often causes the defining clinical sign, and it is located INSIDE the lumen — the options contrast lumen (CN VI) from wall nerves. Exam pearl: Cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with CN III, IV, VI palsies (ophthalmoplegia) + CN V1 sensory loss + proptosis + chemosis + fever. Most common cause: facial/paranasal sinus infection; Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden onset of vertigo, nausea, vomiting, ipsilateral facial numbness, loss of pain and temperature on the opposite limbs, ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, dysarthria, and ipsilateral ataxia of the limbs. Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.explanation: This is the classic Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome caused by PICA occlusion (or vertebral artery occlusion proximal to PICA origin). The lateral medulla is infarcted. Clinical features explained: Ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss — trigeminal spinal nucleus and tract (in lateral medulla). Contralateral limb pain/temperature loss — spinothalamic tract (decussated fibers). Ipsilateral Horner's syndrome — descending sympathetic fibers. Ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia — inferior cerebellar peduncle. Vertigo, nausea, vomiting, nystagmus — vestibular nuclei. Dysphagia, hoarseness — nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X). Note: Corticospinal tract is NOT involved → NO motor (limb) weakness. Option A (AICA) — affects pons and cerebellum; causes ipsilateral facial palsy (CN VII), hearing loss (CN VIII), contralateral limb deficits. Option C (SCA) — affects superior cerebellum and dorsolateral pons; ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia prominent. Option D (Basilar) — 'locked-in' syndrome, quadriplegia, coma, cranial nerve palsies (bilateral). Exam pearl: Wallenberg = Lateral Medullary = PICA; 'Crossed sensory deficit' (face ipsilateral, limbs contralateral) is the hallmark.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man develops sudden onset of wild, flinging movements of the left arm and leg. MRI shows a small infarct in the right subthalamic nucleus. Which neurotransmitter pathway is disrupted, and what is the resultant movement disorder called?

options.A: Loss of dopaminergic input to striatum — Parkinsonism
options.B: Loss of subthalamic nucleus excitation to globus pallidus interna — Hemiballismus
options.C: Loss of GABA-ergic inhibition from striatum to globus pallidus externa — Hemichorea
options.D: Excess dopamine in the striatum — Huntington's disease

questions.explanation: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) normally sends EXCITATORY glutamatergic projections to the globus pallidus interna (GPi). GPi in turn sends inhibitory signals to the thalamus → the thalamus is inhibited, dampening excessive movement. When the STN is destroyed (infarct, trauma): STN excitation of GPi is LOST → GPi is underactive → less inhibition of thalamus → thalamus becomes overactive → excess motor cortex activation → wild, involuntary, high-amplitude, flinging movements of proximal limbs = HEMIBALLISMUS (contralateral to the lesion). This is a hyperkinetic movement disorder. Option A: Loss of dopamine (substantia nigra pars compacta → striatum) → bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor = Parkinsonism (hypokinetic). Option C: Striatum → GPe pathway disruption = part of chorea circuit, not hemiballismus directly. Option D: Huntington's — GABA-ergic striatal neurons lost → excess movement; autosomal dominant, trinucleotide repeat (CAG). Exam pearl: Hemiballismus is the classic result of STN lesion. Most commonly due to small-vessel (lacunar) infarct in the STN, especially in diabetics and hypertensives. Often self-limiting over weeks; treated with haloperidol or tetrabenazine acutely.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.image_title: Spinal Cord Cross-Section with Lesion Zones
key_findings: Demyelination of posterior columns bilaterally
Corticospinal tracts appear normal
Spinothalamic tract signals preserved
Anterior horn cells intact
Subacute onset in a 55-year-old with macrocytic anemia
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old vegetarian woman presents with progressive numbness of the feet, unsteady gait (positive Romberg's sign), and loss of vibration sense. Blood film shows macrocytosis. MRI of spinal cord shows the pattern depicted above (bilateral posterior column involvement). This is subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Which spinal column is primarily affected first?

options.C: Posterior (dorsal) column — fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus

questions.explanation: Subacute combined degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord results from Vitamin B12 deficiency. It characteristically affects the posterior (dorsal) columns first (dorsal column–medial lemniscal pathway): Fasciculus gracilis (lower limbs) and cuneatus (upper limbs) — carry fine touch, vibration, proprioception. Clinical: loss of vibration, loss of proprioception, positive Romberg's sign, pseudoataxia (sensory ataxia — due to proprioception loss, not cerebellar problem). Later involvement: lateral columns (corticospinal tracts) → UMN signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar. 'Combined' because BOTH posterior AND lateral columns affected (not just one). Note: peripheral neuropathy (LMN signs) may also coexist — hyporeflexia + UMN signs = classic B12 deficiency paradox. Spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature) is typically SPARED initially. Cause: strict vegetarianism, pernicious anemia (anti-intrinsic factor antibodies), malabsorption. Option A: Corticospinal tract (anterior column) is affected late in SACD. Option B: Spinothalamic tract is typically spared. Option D: Anterior horn cells affected in motor neuron disease and polio. Exam pearl: B12 deficiency causes SACD + megaloblastic anemia + peripheral neuropathy + psychiatric features.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 68-year-old hypertensive man develops sudden right-sided hemiplegia with face, arm, and leg equally affected, along with right hemisensory loss and hemianopia, but NO cortical signs (aphasia, neglect, agnosia). CT shows a hemorrhage in the left internal capsule. The posterior limb of the internal capsule primarily carries which fibers?

options.A: Frontopontine fibers and anterior thalamic radiations
options.D: Corticobulbar fibers to cranial nerve nuclei

questions.explanation: The internal capsule is organized into the following limbs: Anterior limb: frontopontine fibers, anterior thalamic radiation (to prefrontal cortex). Genu: Corticobulbar (cortical-nuclear) fibers to cranial nerve motor nuclei. Posterior limb: Corticospinal tract (pyramidal motor fibers — upper limb anterior, lower limb posterior), Corticorubral fibers, Somatosensory thalamocortical radiations (posterior part of posterior limb). Retrolenticular part: Optic radiation (lower fibers in Meyer's loop → temporal lobe → lower visual quadrant). Sublenticular part: Auditory radiation, temporopontine fibers. Capsular (pure motor or sensory) strokes are caused by small vessel (lenticulostriate artery) occlusion — NO cortical features because cortex is preserved. Pure motor hemiplegia = posterior limb capsular stroke. The somatotopy in posterior limb: head fibers most anterior, arm next, leg most posterior. Equal face-arm-leg weakness (as in this case) indicates a CAPSULAR lesion, not cortical (which would give arm > face > leg or face > arm in MCA territory). Option A describes anterior limb contents. Option C (optic/auditory radiations) are in the retro/sublenticular portions. Option D (corticobulbar) is at the genu.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old multiparous woman presents with urinary stress incontinence and a sensation of pelvic heaviness. Examination reveals descent of the anterior vaginal wall (cystocele). The primary structural support of the bladder neck and urethra comes from which structure, damage to which causes stress incontinence?
questions.explanation: The pelvic floor (levator ani) is the primary dynamic support structure of the pelvis. In females, it consists of: Puborectalis (most medial, forms the anorectal sling), Pubococcygeus (pubovaginalis, pubourethralis — forms the urogenital hiatus and supports the urethra/vaginal wall), Iliococcygeus (forms the posterior sheet). The pubococcygeus portion (pubovisceralis) provides a 'urethral elevation and support' mechanism. On increases in intra-abdominal pressure (cough, sneeze), normal levator ani contraction simultaneously elevates and compresses the urethra against the pubic symphysis. In multiparous women, obstetric trauma → pudendal neuropathy + levator ani avulsion → loss of this urethral support → stress incontinence and cystocele. Option B: Uterosacral ligaments support the uterus posteriorly; their deficiency → uterine prolapse (apical defect), not stress incontinence directly. Option C: Round ligament of uterus → passes through deep inguinal ring → labia majora; maintains uterine anteversion but provides no pelvic floor support. Option D: External urethral sphincter contributes to urinary continence but cannot alone compensate for loss of anatomical support. Exam pearl: Three levels of vaginal support (DeLancey) — Level I: cardinal/uterosacral (apical/uterine); Level II: paravaginal (anterior/cystocele, posterior/rectocele); Level III: pubourethral/perineal body (most distal support).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman undergoes total abdominal hysterectomy. Postoperatively, she develops fever, right flank pain, and rising creatinine. IVU reveals right-sided hydronephrosis with ureteric obstruction at the level of the cervix. The ureter was most likely injured at which point of anatomical crossing?

options.A: Where the ureter crosses the common iliac artery at the pelvic brim
options.B: Where the ureter passes under the uterine artery ('water under the bridge')
options.C: Where the ureter enters the bladder trigone
options.D: Where the ureter crosses over the ovarian vessels

questions.explanation: The ureter is at greatest risk of injury during hysterectomy at the point where it passes beneath the uterine artery — the classic 'water under the bridge' relationship. The ureter (water) passes UNDER the uterine artery (bridge), approximately 2 cm lateral to the cervix. This is where ligation of the uterine artery during hysterectomy can inadvertently catch the ureter. The ureter is also at risk at: The pelvic brim, where it crosses the common iliac bifurcation (external/internal iliac junction). In the broad ligament. At the anterolateral fornix of the vagina. Option A: Crossing over common iliac at pelvic brim — ureter is at risk here during pelvic lymph node dissection or vascular surgery, but is a less common site of hysterectomy injury. Option C: At the bladder entry — risk during cystectomy, not typical hysterectomy injury. Option D: Crossing over ovarian vessels in the infundibulopelvic ligament — risk during salpingo-oophorectomy ('ureter must be identified before dividing infundibulopelvic ligament'). Exam pearl: The 3 classical danger points for ureteric injury in gynecological surgery: (1) At the pelvic brim over iliac vessels; (2) Beneath uterine artery (most common); (3) At the anterolateral vaginal fornix.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: An obstetrician performs a pudendal nerve block to provide perineal analgesia during vaginal delivery. Where is the pudendal nerve blocked?

options.A: At the sacrospinous ligament, medial to the ischial spine
options.D: In the Alcock's canal, distal to the ischial spine

questions.explanation: The pudendal nerve (S2, S3, S4 — 'S2, 3, 4 keeps the pee and poo off the floor') exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis, hooks around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament, and re-enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen into Alcock's canal (pudendal canal). The pudendal nerve block is performed transvaginally or transperineally by infiltrating local anaesthetic just medial to the ischial spine, where the nerve lies immediately posterior to the sacrospinous ligament attachment. This blocks all three terminal branches: Inferior rectal nerve (external anal sphincter and perianal skin), Perineal nerve (posterior labia, perineal muscles), Dorsal nerve of clitoris. Option B: Ischial tuberosity — too distal; distal branches already separated. Option C: Obturator foramen — obturator nerve territory (medial thigh), not perineal. Option D: Alcock's canal (pudendal canal) is where the nerve travels, but the block is performed at the ischial spine where it's most accessible and superficial. Exam pearl: Pudendal nerve block provides analgesia for the lower vagina, perineum, and vulva — NOT for uterine/cervical pain (those require paracervical block or epidural).

questions.subject: Anatomy
key_findings: Single layer of cells with nuclei at different heights giving a 'stratified' appearance
All cells touch the basement membrane
Cilia visible at the luminal surface
Goblet cells interspersed between columnar cells
Basal cells present near the basement membrane
questions.question_text: The histological image above shows epithelium lining the respiratory tract. A smoker develops squamous metaplasia in the bronchi. Which carcinoma type typically arises from this metaplastic epithelium?
questions.explanation: The respiratory tract (trachea and bronchi) is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (respiratory epithelium) with goblet cells. In chronic smokers, repeated irritation causes squamous metaplasia — the respiratory epithelium is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium (a reversible adaptive change). Continued carcinogenic exposure (smoking) leads to dysplasia → squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the bronchus. SCC is centrally located, arises in major bronchi, is associated with squamous metaplasia, and is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in lung cancer (PTHrP secretion). Option A: Small cell carcinoma — arises from neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells; paraneoplastic syndromes (SIADH, ACTH, Lambert-Eaton); NOT from squamous metaplasia. Option C: Adenocarcinoma — arises from peripheral bronchial glands/Clara cells/alveolar cells; most common lung cancer overall; NOT from squamous metaplasia; more common in non-smokers and women. Option D: Carcinoid — low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, central location, not from squamous metaplasia. Exam pearl: Lung cancer types by location: Central — SCC (most common central; cavitates), SCLC; Peripheral — Adenocarcinoma, Large cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 14-year-old boy with Marfan syndrome undergoes echocardiography showing aortic root dilatation and mitral valve prolapse. The underlying defect involves mutation in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1. Fibrillin forms the core of which extracellular matrix component?
questions.explanation: Elastic fibers consist of two components: Elastin core (crosslinked by lysyl oxidase, gives elastic recoil) and Fibrillin-1 microfibrils (outer sheath; provides structural scaffolding for elastin deposition). In Marfan syndrome, FBN1 mutation (chr 15) leads to defective fibrillin-1 → weakened elastic fiber microfibrils → weakening of aortic media (cystic medial degeneration) → aortic aneurysm, dissection; Mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous degeneration); Lens subluxation (ectopia lentis — zonular fibers are made of fibrillin). Option A: Type I collagen — major structural collagen of bone, tendon, skin, cornea; defective in Osteogenesis imperfecta. Option C: Reticular fibers (Type III collagen) — form the stroma of lymph nodes, spleen, liver sinusoids; defective in Ehlers-Danlos type IV. Option D: Proteoglycan aggregates — ground substance components; relevant in mucopolysaccharidoses. Exam pearl: Marfan syndrome — tall stature, arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, scoliosis, aortic root dilatation, lens subluxation (upward), MVP. Autosomal dominant. FBN1 on chromosome 15 (mnemonic: '15 letters in Marfan syndrome').

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A pathologist examining a specimen notices serous acini with small lumens and darkly staining zymogen granules, along with mucous acini with large pale cells. The serous acini form crescentic caps (demilunes) over the mucous acini. This histological appearance is characteristic of which gland?

options.D: Lingual salivary glands (von Ebner's glands — purely serous)

questions.explanation: The submandibular gland is a mixed gland (both serous and mucous acini), predominantly serous. It characteristically shows serous demilunes — crescentic caps of serous cells (Giannuzzi demilunes) capping the mucous acini. This appearance is unique to the submandibular gland in classic histological descriptions. Option A: Parotid gland — purely serous; produces watery, enzyme-rich saliva; contains large amounts of amylase; large serous acini only. Option B: Sublingual gland — predominantly mucous, with serous demilunes; no purely mucous acini alone (but predominantly mucous overall). The question specifies the mixed nature with prominent serous demilunes, which is most characteristic of the submandibular. Option D: Von Ebner's glands — purely serous; located in the tongue near circumvallate papillae; wash the taste buds. Exam pearl: Salivary gland type order by serous content (most to least serous): Parotid (100% serous) > Submandibular (75% serous, 25% mucous) > Sublingual (predominantly mucous). Parotid duct (Stensen's) opens at upper 2nd molar; Submandibular duct (Wharton's) opens at sublingual papilla.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 10-year-old child is diagnosed with achondroplasia. The growth plates (epiphyseal plates) of long bones show disorganized chondrocyte columnar arrangement with failure of endochondral ossification. The primary defect in achondroplasia involves mutation in:

options.A: Type II collagen gene (COL2A1) — Stickler syndrome
options.B: Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) — gain-of-function mutation

questions.explanation: Achondroplasia is the most common non-lethal skeletal dysplasia. It results from a gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) — a constitutively active (overactive) receptor that normally inhibits chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate. The overactive FGFR3 excessively inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation in the proliferating zone of the growth plate → shorter limbs (rhizomelic shortening — proximal segments shorter), enlarged head (frontal bossing), foramen magnum stenosis, trident hand. Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, but 80% are new mutations (advanced paternal age). Histology of growth plate: Normal zones from epiphysis to diaphysis — Resting (reserve) zone → Proliferating zone (columns) → Hypertrophic zone → Calcification zone → Bone. In achondroplasia, proliferating zone is disorganized/shortened. Option A: COL2A1 mutation → Stickler syndrome (myopia, retinal detachment, cleft palate). Option C: PTH/PTHrP receptor gain-of-function → Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia. Option D: DTDST → diastrophic dysplasia (hitchhiker thumb, scoliosis, cleft palate). Exam pearl: Thanatophoric dysplasia (lethal achondroplasia-like) also involves FGFR3 mutations.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: An emergency physician needs to perform needle decompression for a tension pneumothorax in a 25-year-old trauma victim. At which surface landmark should the needle be inserted?

options.A: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, over the upper border of the 3rd rib
options.C: 2nd intercostal space, midaxillary line, over the lower border of the 2nd rib

questions.explanation: Needle decompression of tension pneumothorax: Insert a large-bore (14G) needle into the 2nd intercostal space (ICS), midclavicular line (MCL), over the UPPER border of the 3rd rib (to avoid the neurovascular bundle — vein, artery, nerve — that runs in the subcostal groove on the lower border of each rib). Why 2nd ICS MCL? The apex of the lung is here; the pleura is accessible; the needle is inserted over the upper border of the 3rd rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle. Alternative site: 4th/5th ICS, anterior axillary line (used in some guidelines, e.g., PHTLS) — less risk of hitting internal mammary vessels. Option B: 5th ICS midaxillary line is the site for chest drain (tube thoracostomy/intercostal drain), NOT needle decompression. Option C: Lower border of the 2nd rib would risk the intercostal neurovascular bundle. Option D: 4th ICS MCL is not the standard landmark for needle decompression. Exam pearl: 'VAN' from top to bottom under each rib: Vein, Artery, Nerve. Always insert needles/drains ABOVE (over upper border of) the rib, not below.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. She has periumbilical bruising (Cullen's sign) and flank bruising (Grey Turner's sign). These signs indicate retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Cullen's sign appears at the umbilicus, which corresponds to which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The umbilicus is a clinically important surface landmark corresponding to the L3–L4 intervertebral disc level (approximately, though ranges from L3–L4 to L4). Structures at this level include: Aortic bifurcation (into left and right common iliac arteries) — occurs at L4. Inferior vena cava formation (junction of common iliac veins) — at L5. The transpyloric plane (important surgical plane) is at L1. Umbilicus dermatome: T10 (the 10th thoracic spinal nerve innervates the skin at the umbilicus — used clinically to test for cord compression). Option A: L1 → transpyloric plane, hilum of kidney, termination of spinal cord (conus medullaris) in adults. Option C: L5 → IVC formation, iliac crest (L4 is 'iliac crest'). Option D: T10 is the DERMATOMAL level of the umbilicus, not the vertebral level of the structure itself. Exam pearl: Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner's sign (flank bruising) indicate retroperitoneal bleeding — causes include acute pancreatitis, ruptured aortic aneurysm, ectopic pregnancy, trauma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A baby is born with a cleft lip. The defect is located on the left side, between the philtrum and the left lateral lip segment. This cleft lip results from failure of fusion between which facial processes?

options.B: Medial nasal process and maxillary process of the 1st pharyngeal arch
options.C: Lateral nasal process and maxillary process

questions.explanation: Cleft lip (cheiloschisis) results from failure of fusion between the medial nasal process (which contributes to the philtrum, prolabium, and central portion of the upper lip) and the maxillary process of the first pharyngeal arch (which forms the lateral portions of the upper lip and cheek). Normal fusion at week 7 of embryonic development forms the upper lip. Cleft palate may coexist if the lateral palatal shelves fail to fuse with the primary palate. Option A: Failure of fusion of two medial nasal processes → midline cleft lip (very rare; median cleft lip), forms the primary palate centrally. Option C: Lateral nasal process and maxillary process fusion → forms the nasolacrimal groove area; failure → oblique facial cleft (very rare). Option D: Mandibular processes fuse in the midline forming the lower lip; failure → midline mandibular cleft (extremely rare). Exam pearl: Lateral cleft lip (most common) = medial nasal + maxillary process failure. Cleft palate (posterior) = failure of lateral palatal shelf elevation and fusion. Combined cleft lip and palate = both failures. Cleft lip can be unilateral (more common, left side) or bilateral.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: At birth, with the first breath and clamping of the umbilical cord, several fetal circulatory shunts close. A newborn is found to have a persistent patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). The ductus arteriosus connects which two vessels in the fetal circulation?

options.B: Ascending aorta and left pulmonary artery
options.D: Superior vena cava and left atrium

questions.explanation: The ductus arteriosus (DA) connects the pulmonary trunk (main pulmonary artery) to the descending aorta (just distal to the left subclavian artery origin). In fetal life, the lungs are non-functional. Most (90%) of right ventricular output (deoxygenated blood) is shunted through the DA from the pulmonary trunk → descending aorta → bypasses the high-resistance pulmonary vasculature → goes to the placenta via umbilical arteries for oxygenation. At birth: Lung expansion → ↑ PO2 → prostaglandin levels fall → DA constricts → closes within 1–2 days → becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. PDA in premature infants: Treated with indomethacin (inhibits prostaglandin synthesis — prostaglandins keep DA open). PGE1 (prostaglandin E1) is used to KEEP the PDA open in duct-dependent congenital heart diseases (e.g., TGA, pulmonary atresia). Option B: Ascending aorta to left pulmonary artery is not the DA. Option C: Pulmonary trunk to left atrium — this is not a structure (foramen ovale connects right to left atrium). Option D: SVC to left atrium — not a cardiac shunt. Exam pearl: Fetal circulation shunts: Foramen ovale (RA→LA), Ductus arteriosus (PA→Aorta), Ductus venosus (umbilical vein→IVC, bypasses liver).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman undergoes axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer. Postoperatively, she develops winging of the scapula. Which nerve was damaged, and which muscle is paralyzed?

options.B: Long thoracic nerve of Bell — serratus anterior

questions.explanation: Winging of the scapula occurs when the medial border of the scapula protrudes posteriorly like a wing. This is caused by paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle, which normally holds the scapula flat against the thoracic wall. The serratus anterior is innervated by the long thoracic nerve of Bell (C5, C6, C7 — 'C5, 6, 7 — bells of heaven'). The long thoracic nerve runs on the superficial surface of serratus anterior on the lateral thoracic wall — vulnerable during axillary dissection, mastectomy, or after carrying heavy loads on the shoulder. The serratus anterior also rotates the scapula upward (glenoid faces upward) for full arm elevation above 90°. Winging is best demonstrated by asking the patient to push against a wall. Option A: Thoracodorsal nerve (C6, C7, C8) — latissimus dorsi; injury during axillary dissection but does not cause winging. Option C: Dorsal scapular nerve — rhomboids; paralysis causes medial winging (different type) with scapula rotating differently. Option D: Accessory nerve — trapezius; injury causes drooping of the shoulder and lateral/rotary winging (shoulder droop when arm raised). Exam pearl: Long thoracic nerve injury = medial winging (scapula medial border wings out); Accessory nerve injury = lateral winging with shoulder drop.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old marathon runner develops medial ankle pain and a flat arch (pes planus) after prolonged running. MRI shows rupture of the spring ligament complex and tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction. The spring (calcaneonavicular) ligament supports which bony component of the medial longitudinal arch?
questions.explanation: The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament runs from the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the inferior surface and tuberosity of the navicular bone. Its upper surface is lined by fibrocartilage and directly supports the head of the talus — the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch. The head of the talus rests upon the spring ligament; when the spring ligament ruptures, the talus sags medially and plantarward, collapsing the medial arch → acquired flatfoot. The medial longitudinal arch (MLA) is the highest arch; its bones: calcaneus → talus → navicular → cuneiforms (1st, 2nd, 3rd) → metatarsals 1–3. Active support: Tibialis anterior (dorsal arch support), Tibialis posterior (sling around navicular, key dynamic support), FHL, Peroneus longus (lateral arch). Passive support: Spring ligament, Plantar fascia, Plantar ligaments (long and short plantar), Intrinsic muscles. Option A: Sustentaculum tali supports the talus superiorly (articular surface). Option C: Navicular tuberosity is the attachment of the tibialis posterior tendon — its avulsion or degeneration is another cause of flat foot. Option D: Medial cuneiform is distal to the navicular; not the structure supported by the spring ligament. Exam pearl: 'Tibialis posterior = keystone of the medial arch' — its tendon dysfunction is the most common cause of adult-acquired flatfoot.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman presents with retraction of the nipple and skin dimpling over the outer upper quadrant of the left breast. Which anatomical structure, when invaded by breast carcinoma, causes the skin dimpling?
questions.explanation: Cooper's ligaments (suspensory ligaments of the breast) are fibrous septa that extend from the overlying skin through the breast stroma to the underlying pectoral fascia. They give the breast its shape and structural integrity. When breast carcinoma invades and shortens these ligaments → the skin is tethered inward → characteristic 'peau d'orange' (orange peel) appearance or focal skin dimpling — a classic sign of malignancy. Similarly, when a carcinoma involves the lactiferous ducts or subareolar tissue → it retracts the nipple (nipple inversion). Lymphatic obstruction → dermal lymphedema → peau d'orange. Option A: Pectoralis major fascia invasion → fixation of the breast to the chest wall (loss of breast mobility), not skin dimpling. Option C: Lactiferous duct involvement → nipple retraction/discharge, not skin dimpling. Option D: Axillary lymphatic channel blockage → arm edema, not breast skin dimpling. Exam pearl: Signs of breast carcinoma: Skin dimpling (Cooper's ligament invasion), peau d'orange (dermal lymphatic obstruction), nipple retraction (duct involvement), hard irregular lump, fixed to skin or deep fascia. The most common quadrant for breast carcinoma: upper outer quadrant (50%).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman develops painless, progressive proptosis of the right eye over 6 months. MRI shows a well-defined intraconal mass. The visual acuity is decreased and optic disc is blurred. The most likely lesion is an optic nerve sheath meningioma. Which space does it occupy, and what is at greatest risk?

options.A: Extraconal space — extraocular muscles are at risk
options.B: Intraconal space — optic nerve compression with visual loss is the primary risk
options.C: Subperiosteal space — globe displacement without vision loss
options.D: Preseptal space — anterior to the orbital septum

questions.explanation: The orbit is divided into compartments by the muscle cone (rectus muscles and their intermuscular membranes): Intraconal space (within the muscle cone): Contains the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, CN III, IV, V1, VI, ciliary ganglion, and orbital fat. Masses here cause AXIAL proptosis (forward displacement of the globe along the visual axis) and early visual loss due to optic nerve compression. Causes: Optic nerve glioma (children — NF1), meningioma, hemangioma (most common benign intraconal tumor in adults), dermoid (extraconal more common). Extraconal space (outside the muscle cone): Contains lacrimal gland, trochlea, orbital fat. Masses cause NON-AXIAL displacement (globe pushed to opposite side) with later visual effects. Visual acuity and optic disc changes confirm optic nerve involvement → intraconal. Option C: Subperiosteal space — between periorbita and orbital walls; often from sinus infection or trauma. Option D: Preseptal — anterior to orbital septum; periorbital cellulitis, not true orbital pathology. Exam pearl: Optic nerve glioma (NF1, children) vs Meningioma (adult females, 'tram-track' calcification on CT). Both intraconal, both cause progressive visual loss.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child presents with an enlarging head circumference (hydrocephalus). MRI shows massive dilatation of the lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle. The cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) appears occluded. What type of hydrocephalus is this, and what is the expected finding on lumbar puncture?

options.A: Communicating hydrocephalus — CSF flows freely from the ventricular system; LP shows elevated opening pressure
options.B: Non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus — LP is dangerous; CSF cannot pass from the ventricles to the subarachnoid space
options.C: Normal pressure hydrocephalus — LP shows normal opening pressure; gait disturbance in elderly
options.D: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo — loss of brain parenchyma causes compensatory enlargement of ventricles

questions.explanation: Aqueductal stenosis (narrowing of the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connecting 3rd and 4th ventricles) causes non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus. Since CSF cannot pass from the 3rd ventricle through the blocked aqueduct to the 4th ventricle → lateral and 3rd ventricles dilate → 4th ventricle is NORMAL in size (key differentiator). The CSF cannot reach the subarachnoid space and spinal cord. LP in this setting is DANGEROUS — it can cause sudden brainstem herniation by reducing the spinal CSF pressure while intracranial pressure remains high (pressure gradient shifts → coning). Treatment: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) or VP shunt. Option A: Communicating hydrocephalus — CSF can pass from ventricles to subarachnoid space but is impaired in reabsorption at arachnoid villi (meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage). LP is less dangerous; CSF drains. Option C: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (Hakim-Adams triad: dementia, gait apraxia, urinary incontinence in elderly); normal LP pressure. Option D: Ex vacuo — not true hydrocephalus; ventricles expand passively after brain atrophy; no increased ICP. Exam pearl: Aqueductal stenosis is the most common cause of congenital obstructive hydrocephalus. X-linked form exists (L1CAM gene mutation).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 3-week-old male infant presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting after every feeding. Olive-shaped mass is palpable in the epigastrium. Ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis. Metabolic workup reveals hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Which biochemical principle explains this acid-base disturbance?

options.A: Loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid below the pylorus
options.B: Loss of hydrochloric acid from the stomach causes metabolic alkalosis; kidneys retain H⁺ to compensate, leading to paradoxical aciduria
options.C: Respiratory compensation causes hypercapnia and worsens acidosis
options.D: Loss of pancreatic alkaline fluid causes metabolic acidosis

questions.explanation: Pyloric stenosis causes repeated loss of gastric contents (HCl-rich, KCl-rich fluid). Pathophysiology: Loss of HCl → less H⁺ in blood → metabolic alkalosis (↑ HCO3⁻). Loss of Cl⁻ → hypochloremia → kidneys reabsorb more HCO3⁻ (to maintain electroneutrality) → worsens alkalosis. Loss of K⁺ → hypokalemia → intracellular shift: K⁺ leaves cells, H⁺ enters cells → less H⁺ in blood → worsens alkalosis. Kidneys paradoxically excrete acidic urine (paradoxical aciduria) to preserve ECF volume and sodium. Why? In hypovolemia, kidneys prioritize Na⁺ reabsorption. In the collecting duct, when K⁺ is depleted, H⁺ is secreted instead of K⁺ in exchange for Na⁺ → aciduria despite systemic alkalosis. Classic electrolytes: ↑ pH, ↑ HCO3⁻, ↓ Cl⁻, ↓ K⁺, ↓ Na⁺. Option A: Below-pylorus loss (intestinal) → HCO3⁻-rich → metabolic acidosis. Option C: Respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis = ↑ PCO2 (hypoventilation), not acidosis. Option D: Pancreatic alkaline loss → metabolic acidosis. Exam pearl: Pyloric stenosis — most common in first-born males; presents at 2–8 weeks; 'string sign' on barium meal; olive mass in epigastrium; treat with Ramstedt pyloromyotomy after correction of metabolic disturbance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man presents with a painless midline neck swelling that moves upward on protrusion of the tongue. The swelling has been present since childhood. The most likely diagnosis is a thyroglossal cyst. This cyst arises from remnants of the thyroglossal duct, which connects the thyroid to:

options.A: The foramen cecum of the tongue to the isthmus of the thyroid
options.C: The pyriform fossa to the thyroid gland
options.D: The hyoid bone to the pretracheal fascia

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland develops from the endoderm of the floor of the primitive pharynx at the foramen cecum (a pit visible at the junction of the anterior 2/3 and posterior 1/3 of the tongue). The thyroid descends through the neck, passing anterior to the hyoid bone (or through it), to its final position in front of the trachea, connected by the thyroglossal duct. Normally the duct obliterates by week 10. A persistent thyroglossal duct forms a cyst anywhere along this path — most commonly below the hyoid bone but above the isthmus, in the midline. The cyst moves upward with tongue protrusion (because it's attached to the foramen cecum via the fibrous remnant) — pathognomonic sign. The cyst also moves with swallowing (attached to pretracheal fascia). Treatment: Sistrunk operation (excise cyst + middle part of hyoid bone — to prevent recurrence, as the duct passes through the hyoid). Option B: Epiglottis to trachea — not related to thyroglossal duct. Option C: Pyriform fossa to thyroid — branchial fistula of 3rd/4th pouch. Option D: Hyoid to pretracheal fascia is part of the path but not the endpoints of the duct. Exam pearl: Thyroglossal cyst must contain thyroid tissue; the only thyroid tissue in some patients → always do a thyroid scan before excision to confirm normal gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 46,XY infant presents with female external genitalia, absent uterus, absent upper vagina, and bilateral undescended gonads in the inguinal region. AMH (anti-Müllerian hormone) levels are elevated. Testosterone is within the male reference range. This is complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS). What accounts for the female phenotype despite XY karyotype and normal testosterone?

options.A: Deficiency of 5-alpha reductase → failure to convert testosterone to DHT in external genitalia
options.B: Non-functional androgen receptor → testosterone cannot act on target tissues; estrogen (from testosterone aromatization) feminizes the external genitalia
options.C: Failure of AMH production → Müllerian structures persist, forming uterus and upper vagina
options.D: Absence of SRY gene → default female development despite XY karyotype

questions.explanation: In CAIS (46,XY), the androgen receptor (AR gene, X-linked) is non-functional. Despite normal testosterone and DHT production: Testosterone cannot act on Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts → Wolffian structures fail to develop (no epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles). DHT (derived from testosterone by 5-alpha reductase in target tissues) cannot act on external genital primordia → no masculinization → female external genitalia. However, the testes are present and functional → Sertoli cells produce AMH → Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts regress → NO uterus or upper vagina. Leydig cells produce testosterone → aromatized to estrogen → estrogen acts (its receptor is normal) → feminization of external genitalia, breast development at puberty. Result: Female phenotype, no uterus (AMH is present and functional), absent axillary/pubic hair (androgen-dependent). Option A: 5-alpha reductase deficiency → XY individual has ambiguous genitalia at birth (but testosterone acts via AR during male development); virilizes at puberty (testosterone rises and DHT increases). Uterus absent (AMH produced), has Wolffian structures (testosterone-dependent). Option C: AMH IS elevated in CAIS — this is what causes Müllerian regression. Option D: SRY is present in XY CAIS (they have normal testes). Exam pearl: CAIS triad — female phenotype, absent uterus, inguinal gonads (testes). Risk of malignant transformation (gonadoblastoma) in undescended testes → gonadectomy after puberty.

questions.subject: Anatomy

Cytoplasm appears to hug surrounding red blood cells (Downey cells)
Irregular nuclear contour with condensed chromatin
Prominent nucleolus absent

questions.question_text: A 19-year-old college student presents with fever, sore throat, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. The peripheral blood smear is shown above. Monospot test is positive. The cells shown (atypical lymphocytes) represent which population responding to EBV infection?

options.B: Activated CD8+ cytotoxic T cells reacting against EBV-infected B cells

questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), which infects B lymphocytes via CD21 (complement receptor). The atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) seen on the blood smear are NOT infected B cells — they are ACTIVATED CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (Tc cells) that are reacting against and attempting to destroy the EBV-infected B cells. These activated T cells are large, with abundant pale cytoplasm that seems to hug surrounding RBCs — characteristic feature. They are called 'reactive' or 'atypical' lymphocytes. The Monospot test (heterophile antibody test) detects IgM antibodies that agglutinate horse/sheep/bovine RBCs. Complications: Splenic rupture (avoid contact sports for 4–6 weeks), airway obstruction (massive tonsillitis), hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, encephalitis, hepatitis. EBV is also associated with Burkitt's lymphoma (c-MYC translocation), Hodgkin lymphoma (Reed-Sternberg cells), nasopharyngeal carcinoma, PTLD. Option A: B cells ARE infected but are smaller; they do not appear as atypical lymphocytes. Option C: NK cells are a minor component. Option D: Plasma cells are derived from B cells but do not appear as Downey cells on smear. Exam pearl: EBV infects B cells (via CD21); T cells (CD8+) react → atypical lymphocytosis seen on smear.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after ingesting organophosphate (OP) pesticide. He presents with bradycardia, excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, miosis, bronchospasm, and muscle fasciculations. The attending physician decides to administer atropine. At which receptor does atropine act to reverse the muscarinic effects, and which OP-induced feature does atropine NOT reverse?

options.A: Atropine blocks nicotinic receptors and does not reverse muscle fasciculations
options.B: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and does not reverse muscle fasciculations (a nicotinic effect)
options.C: Atropine blocks both nicotinic and muscarinic receptors and reverses all features
options.D: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and does not reverse miosis

questions.explanation: Organophosphate poisoning causes irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase → accumulation of ACh at all cholinergic synapses: Muscarinic effects (SLUDGE/DUMBELS): Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation/Diarrhea, GI cramps, Emesis, Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, Miosis. Nicotinic effects (NMJ and autonomic ganglia): Muscle fasciculations, weakness, paralysis; tachycardia (ganglionic stimulation can oppose muscarinic bradycardia). CNS effects: Seizures, coma. ATROPINE: Competitive antagonist at muscarinic (M1, M2, M3) receptors. Reverses all muscarinic features (SLUDGE — dries up secretions, relieves bronchospasm, increases heart rate, dilates pupils). Does NOT reverse nicotinic effects (fasciculations, weakness) — because atropine has no action on nicotinic receptors. For nicotinic effects, pralidoxime (2-PAM) is used — it reactivates acetylcholinesterase if given early (before 'aging'/irreversible OP-enzyme bond). Option A is wrong — atropine does NOT block nicotinic receptors at all. Option C is wrong — atropine has no nicotinic action. Option D is partially wrong — atropine DOES reverse miosis (miosis is muscarinic, mediated by circular smooth muscle of iris via M3 receptors). Exam pearl: OP antidote = Atropine (for muscarinic) + Pralidoxime (2-PAM, for nicotinic/reactivation of AChE, before 'aging'). Diazepam for seizures.
